intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1F (CMT1F) is caused by heterozygous or homozygous mutation in the NEFL gene (162280) on chromosome 8p21.

checks.evidence_quote: Mutations in the NEFL gene were recently reported as a cause for autosomal dominant Charcot-Marie-Tooth type 2E (CMT2E) linked to chromosome 8p21.

paragraphs.text: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1F (CMT1F) is a peripheral neuropathy. It begins early and is often severe, and nerve conduction velocities are moderately to severely slowed (Jordanova et al., 2003). Both dominant and recessive forms have been reported (Abe et al., 2009).

checks.evidence_quote: Patients have an early onset and often a severe clinical phenotype.
checks.explanation: The abstract states that patients with NEFL mutations have an early onset.

checks.claim: CMT1F is often severe.
checks.evidence_quote: Patients have an early onset and often a severe clinical phenotype.
checks.explanation: The abstract states that the phenotype is often severe.

checks.claim: In CMT1F, nerve conduction velocities are moderately to severely slowed.

paragraphs.text: Yum et al. (2009) reported 4 affected children (2 females and 2 males, aged 23, 17, 16, and 13 years) among 5 children of consanguineous Palestinian parents. Symptoms began at about 1.5 years of age. The index patient (II-4) presented at age 2 years with toe walking. The other sibs first showed gait difficulties (II-1 and II-3) or delayed walking (II-5). All 4 affected sibs had infantile hypotonia, distal muscle atrophy and weakness, glove-and-stocking sensory impairment, and absent ankle jerks. Motor milestones were mildly delayed in II-1 and II-3. Pes cavus was present in 3 sibs but not in II-3. Patient II-1 also had moderate proximal leg weakness and a waddling gait, and patient II-4 had mild to moderate proximal arm and shoulder girdle weakness. Patient II-1 had learning difficulties, but the other affected children did not, and 3 of them had normal brain MRIs.

paragraphs.text: On electrophysiologic study, the patients of Yum et al. (2009) had motor nerve conduction velocities of 12 to 25 m/s, within the demyelinating range, and amplitudes became progressively lower with age. In patient II-5, motor conduction velocities were already severely slowed at 4 months. Sensory responses were absent with 2 exceptions: an ulnar response in patient II-3 at age 4 years and a radial response in patient II-5 at age 10. These responses had low amplitudes (4.5 and 17.0 microV, respectively) and slowed conduction velocities (14 and 9 m/s, respectively). Visual evoked responses were prolonged in 3 of 4 patients, which the authors interpreted as subclinical axonal involvement of the CNS. A sural nerve biopsy from patient II-4 showed fewer myelinated axons than normal, with a density of 1300/mm compared to about 6000/mm in normal controls. All myelinated axons were less than 3 microns in diameter and lacked intermediate filaments.

paragraphs.text: Both autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive inheritance have been reported for CMT1F. Jordanova et al. (2003) found a de novo heterozygous NEFL missense mutation in a CMT patient. Abe et al. (2009) found heterozygous missense mutations in 5 unrelated patients and a homozygous nonsense mutation in 1 patient. They concluded that nonsense NEFL mutations probably cause a recessive phenotype, whereas missense mutations cause a dominant phenotype. Yum et al. (2009) reported autosomal recessive inheritance in a consanguineous Palestinian family: the 4 affected sibs were homozygous for a nonsense mutation, and both parents were heterozygous.

paragraphs.text: In 4 affected sibs from a consanguineous Palestinian family with severe early-onset neuropathy, Yum et al. (2009) identified a homozygous c.628G-T transversion in the NEFL gene, resulting in a glu210-to-ter (E210X) substitution. Both parents were heterozygous for the mutation, and the unaffected sib did not carry it. The mutation was not found in more than 11,000 individuals analyzed at a diagnostic laboratory. Yum et al. (2009) expressed the mutant in SW-13 vim- cells. Unlike the dominant Q333P mutant, E210X did not form filaments, accumulated poorly, and did not disrupt filament assembly by wildtype NFL or the vimentin network. The authors concluded that E210X causes a simple loss of function.

paragraphs.text: In a Japanese CMT patient, Abe et al. (2009) identified a homozygous glu140-to-ter (E140X) nonsense mutation in the NEFL gene. They described it as the first homozygous NEFL nonsense mutation to be reported. The patient was one of 223 Japanese CMT patients without mutations in other known CMT genes. Abe et al. (2009) concluded that nonsense NEFL mutations probably cause a recessive phenotype.

paragraphs.text: In 4 affected children of consanguineous Palestinian parents, Yum et al. (2009) identified a homozygous c.628G-T transversion in the NEFL gene, resulting in a glu210-to-ter (E210X) substitution. The children had a severe early-onset neuropathy with infantile hypotonia, distal weakness and sensory loss, and motor conduction velocities of 12 to 25 m/s. Both parents were heterozygous for the mutation, and the unaffected sib did not carry it. The mutation was not found in more than 11,000 individuals analyzed at a diagnostic laboratory. In SW-13 vim- cells, the E210X mutant did not form filaments, accumulated poorly, and did not disrupt filament assembly by wildtype NFL or the vimentin network. The authors concluded that E210X causes a simple loss of function.
